Cave Creek: a desert foothills town with its own water

Cave Creek is an incorporated town in the desert foothills north of Phoenix, and it owns and operates its own water utility. The town bought the system in 2007. Since then, according to its annual water quality reports, it has relied on surface water from the CAP canal, which carries Colorado River water across the desert. A 16 inch raw water pipeline runs more than 12 miles north from the canal to the town's treatment plant, and the town says no wells are currently used to supply that system's drinking water.

The town reports on two systems: the Cave Creek Water System and the Desert Hills Water System. They are reported separately, and the town says the Desert Hills system still draws on wells, supplemented with CAP water, so readings can differ. If you are not sure which serves your home, your water bill or the town's Utilities Department can tell you. The town also runs a wastewater system. Whether your home is on town sewer or a septic system matters if the pool ever has to be drained, so find out before that day comes.

Pool service Cave Creek AZ homeowners ask about

Regular weekly cleaning and maintenance is the steady work: baskets, brushing, vacuuming and testing. Beyond that, Cave Creek calls lean toward pool repair and pump repair, plus filter cleaning for pools that take in desert dust. Water that turns after a storm or a missed week is a job for green pool cleanup.

Hard CAP water and an open desert yard

The town's 2018 water quality report listed hardness of 12 to 15 grains per gallon for the Cave Creek system, with sodium at 91 parts per million. Grains per gallon is the unit most water softener makers use. The U.S. Geological Survey calls water above 180 milligrams per liter very hard, which is about 10.5 grains per gallon. Pool water starts at that level and climbs as the sun evaporates water and refills add more minerals. A pool company that tests calcium hardness along with chlorine and pH can keep that from turning into scale on the tile and inside the equipment.

The yard matters too. A pool open to the desert on one or more sides catches what the wind carries off the lot: dust, leaves, seed pods and bits of dry plant. That shows up as full skimmer baskets, a filter that loads up faster than you expect, and fine silt on the pool floor. During the monsoon season, which the National Weather Service sets as June 15 to September 30, a single dust storm can leave a pool cloudy and the filter pressure high. The monsoon pool care guide covers what to do after one.

Safe checks on a desert lot

  • Clear the baskets. Empty the skimmer basket, and the pump basket with the pump off, after any windy day.
  • Look around the equipment pad. Clear leaves and debris away from the pump and filter so they can cool, and note any drips.
  • Read the filter gauge. Write down the pressure. A jump after a storm usually means the filter needs cleaning.
  • Reset once, then stop. A pool GFCI or breaker that tripped can be reset once. If it pops a second time, stop there and get help.

Pool repair in Cave Creek: what the symptoms usually mean

You do not need to diagnose the problem, only describe it. This table shows what pool companies commonly check first. The company that comes out decides what is actually wrong.

Common pool symptoms and what a pool technician often checks
What you noticeWhat is often checkedRelated page
Pump hums but water does not moveA clogged basket or impeller, a failed motor part, an air leak on the suction sidePump repair
Water level drops faster than evaporationLeaks at the equipment, the plumbing, a light niche or the shellLeak repair
Filter pressure stays high after cleaningWorn or scaled filter media, a partly closed valve, debris in the linesFilter cleaning
Rough, stained or flaking surfaceWater balance history and the age of the plaster or pebble finishRepair or resurface
Heater will not fire or shuts offScale, airflow, water flow and safety switches. Smell gas? Leave the area first.Heater repair

Safety and licensing for Cave Creek repairs

Repair work is where checking the company counts most. Arizona's Registrar of Contractors licenses contractors, and pool equipment, repair and resurfacing work generally calls for a licensed contractor. Ask for the license number and look it up yourself before anyone starts.

Safety first. If you smell gas near a pool heater, leave the area, do not use switches or the heater, and from a safe distance call your gas utility's emergency line or 911. Never mix pool chemicals with each other, keep them stored apart and out of children's reach, and keep children away from a pool that is unfenced, uncovered or too cloudy to see the bottom.

Questions to ask a Cave Creek pool company

  • What is your ROC license number, and what classification is it? Then check it on the ROC search.
  • Is the repair price written down before work starts? Ask for parts and labor separately.
  • How will you handle drained or backwashed water on my lot? Ask which town or HOA rule they follow.
  • Do you test calcium hardness? With very hard fill water, it belongs on every visit's list.

Common questions

Who supplies the water in Cave Creek, AZ?

The Town of Cave Creek does. It bought the water system in 2007 and since then has relied on surface water from the Central Arizona Project (CAP) canal, carried north by a raw water pipeline more than 12 miles long to the town's treatment plant. The town says no wells are currently used to supply drinking water on the Cave Creek system.

How hard is Cave Creek's water?

The town's 2018 water quality report listed hardness at 12 to 15 grains per gallon for the Cave Creek Water System. That counts as very hard. The town posts newer reports for both its Cave Creek and Desert Hills systems on its water quality reports page, so check the one that serves your address.

How do I find pool repair in Cave Creek, AZ?

Call the free line and describe what the pool or equipment is doing. The call goes to an independent pool company that works in Cave Creek. For any repair, equipment, resurfacing or leak work, ask for the company's Arizona ROC license number and look it up on the ROC contractor search before work begins.

Can I drain my pool onto my desert lot in Cave Creek?

Ask before you drain. Rules depend on the town code, any HOA rules and whether your home is on sewer or septic. As a rule of thumb, keep pool water out of washes, streets and neighbors' property, and ask the pool company how it plans to handle the water.

Can I call about a pool problem on a weekend?

Yes. An automated assistant answers the line every hour of every day. If the pool company it connects you with cannot pick up, your details are passed along for a call back.
